1. This Judgment shall decide the instant appeal filed by the appellants under Section 70 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 as amended upto date (hereinafter referred as 'FSS Act') assailing impugned order dated 20.08.2018 passed by Sh. Dharmendra Kumar, the Adjudicating Officer/Addl. District Magistrate (New Delhi), in case file No. ADM(ND)/Case No.
36/FS/2014/140404 in case titled as 'Sh. Bal Mukund v. Akash Tyagi & Ors.' thereby imposing consolidated penalty of Rs. 2 Lakhs over the respondent Nos. 1 to 3 for violation of various provisions of the FSS Act read with provisions of the Food Safety and Standards (Food Products Standard & Food Additives) Regulations, 2011 (hereinafter referred as 'FSS (FPS&FA) Regulation'.

sentences.text:
Briefly stated, it is the case of the appellants that M/s. Jubilant Food Works Ltd. is a company incorporated under the provisions of Companies Act, 1956 having its corporate office at B214,
PhaseII, District Guatum Budh Nagar, Noida201305 and the appellant No.2 Sh. Akash Tyagi was working as Manager at its Restaurant viz., Domino's Pizza India Restaurant situated as N7,
Connaught Place, New Delhi.

It is stated that on 07.05.2014 at around 03:00 p.m. Mr. Bal Mukund,
Food Safety Officer (FSO) accompanied with other staff of the department came at the aforesaid Domino's Pizza Outlet and directly approached the Kitchen area (situated separately from the Restaurant area) where food preparation processes were being carried out; and that the FSO started checking the Kitchen area and went to the shelf where raw Pizza bases were kept prepared by the cook and various ingredients in raw form were kept in the shelf and the FSO took one open container of 'Corn Meal' (which incidentally acknowledges as "Corn Flour" vide Form VA prepared by FSO) kept from the shelf kept for preparing the Pizza Base and took a sample of 'Corn Meal'.

It is the case of the appellants that 'Corn Meal' is used as dusting agent while preparing the pizza base from the dough so that the dough should not stick with the shelf and the only purpose of the 'Corn Meal' is to act as facilitator against the sticky tendency of the dough and 'Corn Meal' is not mixed in any other product or preparation.

It is stated that 'Corn Meal' placed in the container has a shelf life of only three days once it is opened and placed in open container; and though the FSO was informed, he did not bother to take samples from the sealed packets of the 'Corn Meal'.
3. The grievance of the appellants is that the FSO of his own, addressed the sample product as 'Corn Flour' though it was informed to him that sample product was 'corn meal', which is a mixture of various ingredients and he was also informed that it was not meant or available for direct sale to the customers and being used only as intermediary product.

At the cost of repetition, the sample product were seized as per Form VA and other formalities were completed and the Food Analyst later on vide report No FSS/378/2014 dated 25.05.2014 held the sample product to be of 'sub standard' quality because the total ash (on dry weight basis) exceeded the prescribed limit of 0.5 %.

Accordingly, on receipt of the application from the FSO, the Food Business Operator (FBO) i.e. the appellants were served with the notice as per Rule 3.1.1(6) of the Food Safety and Standards Rules,
2011 alongwith copy of the report of the Food Analyst and giving them an opportunity of being heard.

4. It is the case of the appellants that they appeared before the Adjudicating Officer/ADM through Counsel and filed a representation with supporting documents inter alia also submitting copy of the invoice against which sample product was purchased requesting for impleadment of the supplier but the Adjudicating Officer / ADM rejected the application without a speaking order during the course of proceedings despite the fact that the FSO failed to lead any evidence and the fact that the Food Analyst had not explained as to the process of analysis in contravention of Section 46(3) (I) read with 2.4.2 of the FSS (FPS&FA) Regulation, yet the Ld. Adjudicating Officer/ADM passed the impugned order thereby holding the appellants guilty of Section 26(2) (ii) read with Section 3(1) (zx)
of the FSS Act in conjunction with Regulation No. 2.4.7 of (Standards of Corn Flour) of the FSS (FPS&FA) Regulation.
Accordingly, consolidated penalty of Rs. 2 Lakhs was imposed upon the respondent Nos. 1 to 3.

It is pertinent to mention that respondent No.2 Sh. Ajay Kaul has not cared to file the appeal GROUNDS OF APPEAL:

sentences.text:
The impugned order has been assailed by the appellants in the present appeal on the grounds that same is perverse, wrong in law besides arbitrary since the Adjudicating Officer/ADM considered the complaint of the FSO as a gospel truth without verification of facts and evidence in support of the complaint; and that the Adjudicating Officer/ADM overruled the fact that sample product was 'corn meal' (a mixture of various ingredients) and not 'corn flour', and therefore, the application of parameters prescribed for the 'corn flour' under Regulation 2.4.7 of FSS (FPS&FA) Regulation, 2011 vitiated the legal sanctity of the report of the Food Analyst as well as report of the referral Laboratory dated 08.09.2014; and that the Adjudicating Officer/ADM failed to appreciate that the sample product was not meant for "direct sale" to the customers and rather the appellants were consumers of the same; and that neither the appellant respondent no. 2 Ajay Kaul nor respondent no. 3 in the original complaint/ appellant no. 2 herein viz., Akash Tyagi were responsible in any manner for the manufacture and storage of the sample product.
6.

On the filing of the instant appeal, the operation of the impugned order was stayed subject to the appellants submitting a FDR drawn on any nationalized bank for a initial period of one year and to be renewed till further orders, which has been complied with and notice of the appeal was ordered to be issued to the respondent.
Appearance has been put on behalf of the respondents and although no reply as such is filed, the record of the ld Adjudicating Officer is filed and the appeal is opposed.

DECISION:
7. I have given my thoughtful consideration to the submissions made by the ld counsels for the parties at the Bar.

I have meticulously gone through the record of this case including the original record of the ld Adjudicating Officer as also the written submissions filed by the ld counsels for the parties as also the case law cited at the Bar.

In order to deal with the challenges thrown by the appellants, it would be expedient to re produce the operative portion of the impugned order that reads as under: "On the basis of the submissions made and arguments put forward by both sides,

the main issues are as under:
1. Sample commodity was not corn floor and was corn meal.
2. It was not a raw material and was not for sale.
3. It was not sold to FSO.
4. FA report is not valued as method of testing was not given.
5. Sample was not representative and representative sample was not taken.
Since the respondent no.1 himself signed over the form VA at the time of taking of sample whereas sample commodity name was mentioned as Corn Floor.

Not only this but FBO Sh. Akash Tyagi has written in his own handwriting "price of Corn Floor not accepted" at Food Business Operator's Receipt and on Form VA "Corn Floor use in the preparation of Pizza" providing that sample taken was Corn Floor.
I also accept the submission made by the FSO at page 4 & 5 that it is a misrepresentation of the fact corn meal is an admixture of various ingredients.
Neither the accused M/S Jubilant Foodworks Ltd vs Sh. Bal Mukund on 13 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/19460410/

sentences.text: 3 No.1 at the time of sampling not the defendants through their representation before adjudication officer have disclosed the so called other ingredients.

As per various definitions available in Wikipedia and other dictionaries, MEAL is a course ground grain whereas Flour is fine ground grain, so standards of corn floor are applicable in either case i.e. corn or corn meal as prescribed in Regulation 2.4.7 of FSS (Food Products Standard & Food Additives) Regulations, 2011.

entities.text: FSS (Food Products Standard & Food Additives) Regulations, 2011
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text:
Further,
That corn flour is not a natural primary product but it is processed corn and its result of parameters depends upon the various factors like proper storage and cleanliness etc and total ash can increase if the food article is having impurities and is not cleaned properly before processing.
Further, the respondents had taken opportunity as per section 46(4) of FSS Act for sending one counter part of sample to RFL for analysis.
Accordingly, RFL Mysore had also tested the sample as Corn Flour and found the sample substandard vide their report no.127F/FSSA/2014 dated 08/09/2014.

He had also opined that sample does not conform to the standards laid down for Corn Flour under the provisions of FSS (Food Products Standard and Food Additives) Regulation 2011 as claim of claimant does not sustained.

entities.text: FSS (Food Products Standard and Food Additives) Regulation 2011
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: Definition of Food as mentioned in Section 3.1(j) of FSS Act empowered FSO to take sample.

On perusal of panchnama which was prepared during the taking of sample duly signed by the respondent no.1, it has been found that a sum of Rs.60/ was offered to the FBO as a price of commodity sample bu same was not accepted by the FBO so their claim reg. payment of sample not sustained.
Their claim reg. representative of sample does not sustained as FAC order are not applicable in FSS Act.

The arguments forwarded by Ld. Counsel in regard to difference of 0.3% in results leading to non representative nature of sample is also not correct as the citations pertains to different case related to presence of salt in coriander powder titled as Kashinath vs State whereas the present case is presence of ash in Corn Floor I have sought opinion of two Directors of referral lab in a case pending before me titled as FSO vs M/s Durga Paneer Bhandar & Ors.

entities.text: FSO vs M/s Durga Paneer Bhandar & Ors
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Both the directors have opined that there is no reason in holding a sample 0.3%.
They have confirmed that there is no literature in this regard nor there is any logic.
Further the previous judgments of Hon'ble Courts is based on Food Adulteration Act whereas this case is under the FSS Act 2006.
This Act has a provision that findings of referral labs will be final.
So there is no question of judging nature of sample on the basis of results of two labs.
The defendants have also filed an application for impleadment of manufacturer of sample product.

That application has been rejected by my predecessor there was no cogent reason for accepting the request when opportunity had already been lost when that opportunity was provided by FSO/DO."
8.
At the outset on a careful perusal of the impugned order and on a conspectus of the record of this case, I find the instant appeal is bereft of any merits.

The reasons are not far to seek and let us deal with the contentions raised by the Ld. counsel for the appellants.
NATURE OF THE SAMPLE PRODUCT M/S Jubilant Foodworks Ltd vs Sh. Bal Mukund on 13 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/19460410/
4 9.

entities.text: NATURE OF THE SAMPLE PRODUCT M/S Jubilant Foodworks Ltd vs Sh. Bal Mukund
entities.label: PETITIONER

sentences.text: There is no infirmity or illegality in the impugned order in so far as the sample product is held to be 'corn flour' and not 'corn meal'.

First thing first, the sample product is a 'food item' within the meaning of section 3(1)(j) of the FSS Act that defines the term 'food' to mean "any substance,
whether processed, partially processed or unprocessed, which is intended to be used for human consumption and includes primary food, to the extent defined in clause (zk)".
(the whole definition is skipped as it is not relevant).

In so far as section 3(1) (zk) of the FSS Act is concerned, it defines 'primary food' to mean "an article of food, being a produce of agriculture....resulting from growing ,
raising, cultivation, picking , harvesting .."

Without further ado, the sample article was not a natural primary product but a 'processed corn" and in the own words of the appellants, a food items used in the preparation of the end product by the FBO(Food Business Operator) for sale to the customers.
The sample product was an essential part the cooking process and there is no merit in the plea of the appellants that it was a 'corn meal' which was claimed to be a mixture of various ingredients.

The ld Adjudicating Officer rightly observed that the claim by the appellants that the sample product was a mixture of various ingredients was not substantiated since there was led no iota of evidence as to what were the ingredients.

It is but a matter of common knowledge for those who know little bit of cooking that the sample product was makki ka aata or corn starch powder, which has a good binding capacity and is commonly used in kitchen for cooking purposes, somewhat similar to use of 'wheat flour' used while baking a roti, chapati or parantha etc. so as to take care of the sticky nature of the dough.
In northern India is called "palothan" and, indeed the sample product was a dusting agent or facilitator but certainly not in the nature of 'corn meal'.
LABORATORY ANALYSIS 10.

The standards for corn flour is provided by Regulation 2.4.7 of the FSS (FPS&FA) Regulations which reads as under: "2.4.7 CORNFLOUR (Maize starch)
1. CORNFLOUR (Maize starch) means the starch obtained from maize (zea mays L.).
It shall contain no added colour, flavours or other chemicals.
It shall be free from dirt, insects, larvae and impurities or other extraneous matter.
It shall conform to the following standards: Moisture Not more than 12.5% Total ash Not more than 0.5 per cent (on dry weight basis).
Ash insoluble in dilute HCl Not more than 0.1 per cent (on dry weight basis).

Alcoholic acidity Shall be equivalent to not more than 2.0 ml. (with 90 per cent alcohol) N. NaOH per 100 g. of dried substance."
11.
It is a matter of record that the corn flour (maize starch powder) used and lifted as sample in this case was found to be substandard as per laboratory report dated 22.05.2014.

As per the said report, it was opined that the 'total Ash content was found to be 1.28% on analysis as per DGHS Manual which was more than the prescribed standard of 0.5% (on dry weight basis) beside the fact that Alcoholic acidity (with 90 percent alcohol) per 100 gram of dried substance), which was supposed to be 0.5ml, was found to be more than 2.0ml N NaOH on analysis as per DGHS Manual.

It is pertinent to mention herein that as per Section 46(3) of FSS Act, the Food Analyst is enjoined upon to analysis the sample sent by the FSO within 14 days from the date of collection, which was M/S Jubilant Foodworks Ltd vs Sh. Bal Mukund on 13 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/19460410/
5 admittedly done on 07.05.2014.
12.

sentences.text: There is no merit in the plea raised by the ld. counsel for the appellants as regard violation of Regulation 2.4.2 of FSS (FPS & FA) Regulations, 2011, since the Food Analyst has clearly indicated that the method of analysis was as per DGHS Manual.

As a matter of fact, it is clearly borne out from the record of the Ld. AO/ADM that on the request of the appellants, the sample product was sent for further analysis to the Referral Food Laboratory, CFTRI, Mysore, whereby the sample product was received on 30.06.2014; and as per the report vide the prescribed Form A in terms of Regulation 2.3.1. of Food Safety & Standard (Laboratory & Sample Analysis) Regulation 2011, dated 08.09.2014, the Ash content was found to be 1.1, which was over and above the prescribed limit of 0.5% besides the Alcoholic acidity % by dry weight basis, which should not have been more than 2ml but was found to be 10ml.

entities.text: Food Safety & Standard (Laboratory & Sample Analysis) Regulation 2011
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text:
The appellants' plea that the sample product had exceeded its shelf life,
again cuts no ice as it was on the joint request of the appellants as well as the FSO that the sample product was referred to further analysis at Mysore Laboratory, which report assumes finality in terms of Regulation 2.4.6 of FSS (FPS & FA) Regulations, 2011.
13. Further, the plea by the appellants that the sample product lifted by the FSO was not meant for direct sale does not cut much ice either.
At the cost of repetition, the sample product which was 'Corn Flour' was a food item within the meaning of Section 3(1)(j) of FSS Act.

The appellants were in the business of 'food business' within the meaning of Section 3(1)(n) of FSS At as the sample product was used in relation to an activity relating to the stage of manufacture and processing of final food item by the Food Business Operator (in short 'FBO') as defined by Section 3(1)(o) of FSS Act.

This Court could not agree more with the submission of the Ld. Chief PP for the State who canvassed the plea that the sample product was used for "sale" within the meaning of Section 3(1)(zr) of FSS Act meaning thereby that it was in the nature of sale of an article of food in retail, for human consumption and the sample product viz., "Corn Flour" was substandard within the meaning of Section 3(1)(zx) of FSS Act.

14. Incidentally, the plea of the appellants that the sample product was not meant for direct sale does not merit any consideration either since Chapter VI vide Section 26 of FSS Act provides for the responsibility of the Food Business Operator and vide Section 26(2) of FSS Act, "no FBO is allowed to manufacture, store, sell or distribute any article of food which is misbranded or substandard or contain extraneous matter".

The fact of the matter is that by using the 'Corn Flour' during the cooking process to take care of the dough for finally coming out with the end preparation of Pizza by the appellants, the appellants were in violation of Section 27 of FSS Act too, as it kept 'Corn Flour' in an open container, not identifiable as to its manufacturer or its distributor from whom such article of food was received.

The Ld. AO/ADM rightly observed that the FSO attempted to pay Rs.60/
after taking the sample of the 'Corn Flour', which was reflected in the Form VA signed by appellant no. 2 without any demur or protest and the offered amount was not accepted by him/FBO.

15. Much mileage was sought to be taken by the Ld. Counsel for the appellants by referring to defences available vide Section 80 of FSS Act urging that it was not the manufacturer of the sample product but its ends user and that it had no knowledge that the 'Corn Flour' was substandard.

sentences.text: 6 The conditions in Section 80(B)(2)(b)(ii) of FSS Act were not satisfied by the appellants as despite reasonable time at their disposal they failed to produce any evidence before the FSO as also before the Ld. AO/ADM as to who was the supplier of the 'Corn Flour' and no bills or invoices were produced in this regard.

Although a feeble attempt was made at the fag end of the proceedings before the Ld. AO/ADM to implead the supplier/ manufacturer but the application was rightly rejected by the Ld. AO/ADM as no proof was provided with regard to the sample product and the so called manufacturer/supplier.

The crux of the matter is that the appellants being the FBO was under a paramount duty to ensure that any primary or processed food used for preparation of the dough or for using the 'Corn Flour' as facilitator as against the sticky nature of dough, the product should have been such that was meeting the prescribed parameters in terms of Regulation 2.4.7 of FSS (FPS&FA) Regulations, 2011.
POWERS OF THE FSO 16.

It was then also urged by the Ld. Counsel for the appellants that FSO had no power to enter into the kitchen of the appellants and lift the sample in the manner he did and the proceedings conducted by him vide prescribed Form VA were not in conformity with law.

The plea is recorded only to be shot down since the powers of FSO are categorically delineated under Section 38 of the FSS Act, "who may take a sample of any food, or any substance, which appears to him to be intended for sale, or to have been sold for human consumption or to take any article of food or substance which is found by him on or in any such premises".

17. Lastly, the plea that the sample product was not representative or that representative sample was not taken, also holds no water since admittedly the sample was taken by the FSO from an open plastic container bearing no label declaration as reflected in the prescribed Form VA, which was acknowledged by accused no.2.

There were kept no sealed container of 'Corn Flour' at the time of taking sample from the premises in question and it is in the said context that the belated application by the appellants for impleading the manufacturer/ supplier was disallowed as they have been unable to establish any link by producing any bills or invoices.
CASE LAW RELIED UPON BY THE APPELLANTS / CASE LAW DISTINQUISHABLE 18.
Before parting with this appeal, I would be failing in my duty if I do not reflect on the case law relied upon by the appellants.

It is but well ordained in legal jurisprudence that no ratio, decision or proposition of law given in a case decided by the superior courts can be read or applied de hor the contextual background or the facts and circumstances of that particular case before the superior court, for which reference can be invited to decision in Padma Sundara Rao v State of Tamil Nadu,
(2002) 3 SCC 533.

sentences.text:
The case law examined from the said perspective, I am afraid the ratio in the case Pepsico India Holdings Private Limited v Food Inspector and Another, 2010 (2) FAC 310 is inapplicable since it was a case where the prosecution was launched under the old Act i.e.
Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, where the entire controversy hinged on the fact that no specific limit had been prescribed for Sweetened Carbonated Water under Rule 65 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules 1955.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The prosecution was quashed since no standards were prescribed for packaged drinking water under the relevant regulations/rules and also for the fact that the Central Government had also failed to frame rules to define the laboratories where the sample of M/S Jubilant Foodworks Ltd vs Sh. 7 food could be analyzed by the Public Analyst, or to define the validated methods of analysis and the liability of its directors.
19. Reference was invited to decision in Majid Hussain Zamali, Food Inspector v Ramlal Sahu, 1998 (I) FAC 153, wherein a sample of milk was lifted from a tea shop and it was found that the tea vendor was not selling the milk but tea only.

sentences.text: Further, the said decision was given in the context of Rule 18 of the Food Adulteration Rules, which is not applicable to the facts of the instant case.

Ld. 
Counsel for the appellants then referred to the decision in B. Govindra Rao vs. V.N. Ashokan, 2003 (2) FAC 123, which was in the context of Section 7 & 16 of Prevention of Food Adulteration Act,
1954, which provided that sample could only be taken from the article of food which is manufactured, stored or exposed for sale.

entities.text: B. Govindra Rao vs. V.N. Ashokan, 2003 (2) FAC 123
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It was a case where red cherry kept in the store was found to be not intended for sale in a restaurant run by the FBO.

At the cost of repetition, it was a decision in the context of Section 16(1)(a) of Food Adulteration Act, whereby it was held that storage or distributor of an article of food for a purpose other than for a sale does not fall within the mischief of said Section.

Counsel for the appellants then placed reliance on decision in M.N. Choudhary v State of Bihar, 2007 (I) FAC 106, where a sample of iodized salt was collected from the premises of the Hotel and the prosecution was launched against the General Manager of the Hotel, who was neither the person incharge of the affairs of the store nor of the kitchen of the Hotel, and in the said circumstances, the prosecution against him was quashed inter alia also on the ground that the storage of iodized salt which was not meant for direct sale was not coming within the mischief of Section 16(1) of Food Adulteration Act, 1954.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
Likewise, decision in Hindustan Lever Ltd v Nayak,
Food Inspector, 2021 (1) FAC 320 was cited, which was a case of selling adulterated flora refined sunflower oil in contravention of Section 7(1) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, and the prosecution launched was quashed primarily on the ground of not explaining the method of analysis under Section 23(1A) (hh) of PFA Act.

entities.text:
Hindustan Lever Ltd v Nayak,
Food Inspector, 2021 (1) FAC 320
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Suffice to state that the Ld. AO/ADM has rightly observed in the impugned order that the cited judgments were in relation to the provision of the old act viz., the Food Adulteration At, 1954, and inapplicable in view of the entirely different legal framework of the FSS Act, 2006.

21. In view of the foregoing discussion, there is no escape from the conclusion that the appellants being the FBO were under a statutory responsibility to sell to the customers a final product for human consumption after rigorously processing the food product through various ingredients of standardized food items including 'Corn Flour', which substance was integral to the process of cooking and the prosecution has clearly brought home that the appellants were using a sub standard item which was not in conformity with the prescribed standards for usage of Corn Flour in terms of Regulation 2.4.7 of FSS (FPS & FA) Regulations, 2011.
22.

All said and done, the only blemish in passing the impugned order by the Ld. AO/ADM is about privately seeking opinion of two directors of referral laboratories in some other cases pending before him and holding that there was no literature on the subject.
Be that as it may, the said blemish has neither caused any apparent or real prejudice to the appellants nor it has resulted in any miscarriage of justice since the impugned order of the Ld. AO/ADM

is otherwise based on transparent and M/S Jubilant Foodworks Ltd vs Sh. Bal Mukund on 13 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/19460410/
8 cogent reasons in conformity with law and rules and regulations framed under the FSS Act.
23.

sentences.text: In view of the foregoing discussions, the present appeal is dismissed.

The impugned order dated 20.08.2018 holding the appellants violating the provisions of Section 26(2)(ii) read with section 3(1)(zx) of FSS Act and Regulation 2.4.7 of FSS (FPS & FA) Regulations, 2011, punishable u/s 51 of FSS Act, is upheld.

There are no compelling reasons to interfere with the consolidated penalty of Rs.
2 lakhs imposed upon the appellants for storing, manufacturing and selling the substandard product.
The FDR placed on the record equivalent to the amount of penalty be released in favour of the department/respondent for realization of amount of penalty.
The Record of the Ld. AO/ADM be returned along with the copy of the order.
24. File of appeal be consigned to the Record Room.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
There is no infirmity or illegality in the impugned order in so far as the sample product is held to be 'corn flour' and not 'corn meal'.
First thing first, the sample product is a 'food item' within the meaning of section 3(1)(j) of the FSS Act that defines the term 'food' to mean "any substance,
whether processed, partially processed or unprocessed, which is intended to be used for human consumption and includes primary food, to the extent defined in clause (zk)".
Without further ado, the sample article was not a natural primary product but a 'processed corn" and in the own words of the appellants, a food items used in the preparation of the end product by the FBO(Food Business Operator) for sale to the customers.
The sample product was an essential part the cooking process and there is no merit in the plea of the appellants that it was a 'corn meal' which was claimed to be a mixture of various ingredients.
The ld Adjudicating Officer rightly observed that the claim by the appellants that the sample product was a mixture of various ingredients was not substantiated since there was led no iota of evidence as to what were the ingredients.
It is but a matter of common knowledge for those who know little bit of cooking that the sample product was makki ka aata or corn starch powder, which has a good binding capacity and is commonly used in kitchen for cooking purposes, somewhat similar to use of 'wheat flour' used while baking a roti, chapati or parantha etc. so as to take care of the sticky nature of the dough.
As a matter of fact, it is clearly borne out from the record of the Ld. AO/ADM that on the request of the appellants, the sample product was sent for further analysis to the Referral Food Laboratory, CFTRI, Mysore, whereby the sample product was received on 30.06.2014; and as per the report vide the prescribed Form A in terms of Regulation 2.3.1. of Food Safety & Standard (Laboratory & Sample Analysis) Regulation 2011, dated 08.09.2014, the Ash content was found to be 1.1, which was over and above the prescribed limit of 0.5% besides the Alcoholic acidity % by dry weight basis, which should not have been more than 2ml but was found to be 10ml.
The appellants' plea that the sample product had exceeded its shelf life,
again cuts no ice as it was on the joint request of the appellants as well as the FSO that the sample product was referred to further analysis at Mysore Laboratory, which report assumes finality in terms of Regulation 2.4.6 of FSS (FPS & FA) Regulations, 2011.
13. Further, the plea by the appellants that the sample product lifted by the FSO was not meant for direct sale does not cut much ice either.
At the cost of repetition, the sample product which was 'Corn Flour' was a food item within the meaning of Section 3(1)(j) of FSS Act.
The appellants were in the business of 'food business' within the meaning of Section 3(1)(n) of FSS At as the sample product was used in relation to an activity relating to the stage of manufacture and processing of final food item by the Food Business Operator (in short 'FBO') as defined by Section 3(1)(o) of FSS Act.
This Court could not agree more with the submission of the Ld. Chief PP for the State who canvassed the plea that the sample product was used for "sale" within the meaning of Section 3(1)(zr) of FSS Act meaning thereby that it was in the nature of sale of an article of food in retail, for human consumption and the sample product viz., "Corn Flour" was substandard within the meaning of Section 3(1)(zx) of FSS Act.
The fact of the matter is that by using the 'Corn Flour' during the cooking process to take care of the dough for finally coming out with the end preparation of Pizza by the appellants, the appellants were in violation of Section 27 of FSS Act too, as it kept 'Corn Flour' in an open container, not identifiable as to its manufacturer or its distributor from whom such article of food was received.
It is but well ordained in legal jurisprudence that no ratio, decision or proposition of law given in a case decided by the superior courts can be read or applied de hor the contextual background or the facts and circumstances of that particular case before the superior court, for which reference can be invited to decision in Padma Sundara Rao v State of Tamil Nadu,
(2002) 3 SCC 533.
21. In view of the foregoing discussion, there is no escape from the conclusion that the appellants being the FBO were under a statutory responsibility to sell to the customers a final product for human consumption after rigorously processing the food product through various ingredients of standardized food items including 'Corn Flour', which substance was integral to the process of cooking and the prosecution has clearly brought home that the appellants were using a sub standard item which was not in conformity with the prescribed standards for usage of Corn Flour in terms of Regulation 2.4.7 of FSS (FPS & FA) Regulations, 2011.
22.
Be that as it may, the said blemish has neither caused any apparent or real prejudice to the appellants nor it has resulted in any miscarriage of justice since the impugned order of the Ld. AO/ADM
opennyai_summary.decision:
In view of the foregoing discussions, the present appeal is dismissed.
The impugned order dated 20.08.2018 holding the appellants violating the provisions of Section 26(2)(ii) read with section 3(1)(zx) of FSS Act and Regulation 2.4.7 of FSS (FPS & FA) Regulations, 2011, punishable u/s 51 of FSS Act, is upheld.
There are no compelling reasons to interfere with the consolidated penalty of Rs.
2 lakhs imposed upon the appellants for storing, manufacturing and selling the substandard product.
The FDR placed on the record equivalent to the amount of penalty be released in favour of the department/respondent for realization of amount of penalty.
The Record of the Ld. AO/ADM be returned along with the copy of the order.
24. File of appeal be consigned to the Record Room.
